hook.text: Throw food scraps in a pile, wait a few months, and you get black gold—rich, crumbly compost.

buildup.text: Bacteria and fungi break down organic waste into humus. Heat builds inside the pile—up to 160°F.

discovery.text: That heat kills weed seeds and pathogens. Finished compost is safe, stable, and packed with nutrients.

twist.text: Bad composting stinks. Without enough air or carbon-rich material, anaerobic bacteria take over and produce methane.

climax.text: Large-scale composting diverts millions of tons of waste from landfills and turns it into soil amendment.

punchline.text: Waste in, wealth out. Composting turns trash into soil.

quiz.question: What kills weed seeds and pathogens during composting?
options: High heat generated by microbial activity inside the pile

details.summary: Composting is the controlled biological decomposition of organic waste into a stable, nutrient-rich soil amendment called compost. This topic covers the science of composting—carbon-to-nitrogen ratios, temperature phases, moisture management—and its role in building soil health.
details.whyItMatters: Composting recycles organic waste into a powerful soil amendment that improves structure, water retention, and fertility. It reduces landfill waste and methane emissions while providing a sustainable alternative to synthetic fertilizers.
takeaways: Effective composting requires a carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of roughly 25-30 to 1
Thermophilic composting reaches 55-70°C, killing pathogens, weed seeds, and parasites
Finished compost improves soil structure, water retention, and nutrient availability

faq.question: What is the science behind the composting process?
faq.answer: Composting is aerobic microbial decomposition. Bacteria and fungi consume organic matter, generating heat. The process moves through mesophilic (20-45°C), thermophilic (45-70°C), and curing phases. Proper carbon-to-nitrogen ratios, moisture (40-60%), and oxygen supply drive efficient decomposition.

faq.question: How does compost improve agricultural soil?
faq.answer: Compost adds stable organic matter that improves soil structure and porosity. It increases water-holding capacity by up to 20%. It slowly releases nitrogen, phosphorus, and micronutrients. It feeds beneficial soil organisms, suppresses some soil-borne diseases, and buffers soil pH.
